system:
You are an impartial methodological referee for a biomedical data-analysis agent. Two candidate analysis plans for the same scientific question have each been run at small scale. For each plan you receive its design and an evidence card: numbered facts measured in that pilot run and facts about how the plan validated itself. Decide which plan, if run in full, is more likely to give a valid answer to the question, with a conclusion that matches its evidence.

How to judge
1. Judge only from the objective and the evidence cards. Every reason you give must cite evidence ids; an argument without an id does not count.
2. Complexity is not a reason. That a method sounds advanced, modern or powerful counts for nothing; what it demonstrably did in the pilot counts.
3. A higher self-reported score is not sufficient. Each score was produced under that plan's own validation design. Read the validation-design items and ask what the score would mean under a strict design: Was the scoring target smoothed or cleaner than the real one? Was a configuration picked on the very folds that are reported? How many configurations did each comparison arm get? Is there any measure of spread, and is the difference between the plans larger than it?
4. Convergence. A model that had not converged has not shown what it can do, and its score is unreliable in both directions. Prefer evidence from converged training; do not reward an unconverged model for a promising number.
5. The comparison with the rulers and the simple reference on the same data matters more than the absolute score.
6. Fitness for the question. Prefer the plan whose design can actually deliver what the objective asks for (the estimand, the required comparators, the permitted conclusion).
7. Cost is a tie-breaker, and a disqualifier only when a full run would not fit the stated budget.
8. Declare a tie only when the evidence does not separate the plans.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"winner": "first" | "second" | "tie",
 "cited_evidence": [evidence ids you relied on],
 "reason": "at most 120 words, citing ids inline",
 "validity_concerns": {"first": [short strings], "second": [short strings]}}
text:
{"winner": "first",
 "cited_evidence": ["P6-E2", "P6-E3", "P6-E4", "P6-E5", "P6-E6", "P6-E8", "P6-E10", "P2-E2", "P2-E3", "P2-E4", "P2-E5", "P2-E6"],
 "reason": "Both pilots converged (P6-E5, P2-E5) and both scored against thinned unsmoothed halves with nested early stopping (P6-E6, P2-E6). On the same cells, P6 beats the cluster-mean floor by +0.0114 (CI +0.0100 to +0.0130; P6-E3). That margin is far larger than its 0.0003 SD (P6-E1), and P6 calls 255 genes in Group 2 (P6-E4). P2 falls below the cluster-mean floor (-0.0021, CI excludes 0; P2-E3) and below ridge by 0.0164 (P2-E2). It calls only 5 genes (P2-E4), so its learned model adds nothing beyond cell identity. P6 only ties ridge (-0.0008; P6-E3), so its complexity is unjustified, and the executor ignored some of its settings (P6-E10). Its full run still fits the budget (P6-E8).",
 "validity_concerns": {"first": ["no gain over ridge simple learner (-0.0008), complexity not justified per A5", "executor ignored member training settings (inner_val_fraction, meta alphas, convergence audit)", "only 2 of 9 splits in pilot; SD from 2 splits", "Group 2 calls may largely reflect what ridge already captures"],
  "second": ["significantly below cluster-mean baseline", "well below ridge simple learner", "near-empty gene set would misattribute failure to biology rather than model", "only 2 of 10 splits in pilot"]}}

json.reason: Both pilots converged (P6-E5, P2-E5) and both scored against thinned unsmoothed halves with nested early stopping (P6-E6, P2-E6). On the same cells, P6 beats the cluster-mean floor by +0.0114 (CI +0.0100 to +0.0130; P6-E3). That margin is far larger than its 0.0003 SD (P6-E1), and P6 calls 255 genes in Group 2 (P6-E4). P2 falls below the cluster-mean floor (-0.0021, CI excludes 0; P2-E3) and below ridge by 0.0164 (P2-E2). It calls only 5 genes (P2-E4), so its learned model adds nothing beyond cell identity. P6 only ties ridge (-0.0008; P6-E3), so its complexity is unjustified, and the executor ignored some of its settings (P6-E10). Its full run still fits the budget (P6-E8).

first: no gain over ridge simple learner (-0.0008), complexity not justified per A5
executor ignored member training settings (inner_val_fraction, meta alphas, convergence audit)
only 2 of 9 splits in pilot; SD from 2 splits
Group 2 calls may largely reflect what ridge already captures
second: near-empty gene set would misattribute failure to biology rather than model
